episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Williams
episodes.lead: The lynching of Charles Williams took place on the night of July 4, 1885, when twelve or fifteen men took Williams, a Black prisoner, from two constables on the road to Laurens Court House, South Carolina, and shot him to death. Williams had been arrested for an alleged attempt to "ravish" a young white girl and was protesting his innocence when he was seized. No arrests were reported, and the killing drew notice a month later when the Charleston News and Courier sent a correspondent to investigate a series of violent incidents in Laurens County.

episodes.title: Whipping death of a farm laborer in Lincoln County, Georgia
episodes.lead: The whipping death of a farm laborer in Lincoln County, Georgia, took place in 1885, before July 29, when two sons of the planter Joseph Dill gave 500 lashes to a Black man who had demanded his unpaid wages. He died soon afterward; an inquest called it murder, but the grand jury ignored the bill. The New York Freeman cited the case among Georgia's unpunished killings of Black people.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jack Hopkins
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jack Hopkins took place in Monticello, Jasper County, Georgia, in the last days of July 1885, when masked men shot Hopkins, a Black prisoner, to death through the openings of his jail cell. Hopkins had been arrested days earlier, accused of knifing his employer or a young white man. A coroner's jury attributed the death to unknown parties, and the killing ran in white papers across the country, some calling it a lynching and others the fate of a 'murderer'.

episodes.title: Shooting of a Black soldier by the Hastings city marshal
episodes.lead: The shooting of a Black soldier by the Hastings city marshal took place in Hastings, Nebraska, around the middle of July 1885, when the town's city marshal shot a man described only as "the negro soldier." The soldier survived, and by early August he was reported to be recovering and to have gone to join his regiment.

episodes.title: Lynching of Howard Cooper
episodes.lead: The lynching of Howard Cooper was the hanging of a Black man by a mob at Towsontown, Maryland, some time before July 25, 1885, after he was accused of assaulting a white girl. He was hanged from a sycamore tree, which curiosity seekers later carried off in pieces. The surviving coverage concerns the aftermath: Black protest and a false rumor that Black men would attack Towsontown in revenge.

episodes.title: Waterloo attack on emigration agent John Milam
episodes.lead: The Waterloo attack on emigration agent John Milam took place on the evening of July 20, 1885, when white residents of Waterloo, Laurens County, South Carolina, drove off a railway agent who had come to take six Black women to Arkansas. Milam's own account, carried by an Atlanta wire, said a mob shot at him, tied and beat him, while Waterloo residents said he was only warned and fled after shots fired in the air. Black newspapers presented the case as proof that white Southerners would use force to keep Black laborers from leaving.

episodes.title: Whipping of Jim Caskey
episodes.lead: The whipping of Jim Caskey was an attack on a Black man by a band of forty masked men near Douglass Church in Newberry County, South Carolina, on or about July 31, 1885. The men gave Caskey 200 lashes, ordered him to leave the county within twenty-four hours, and also went looking for a second Black man, Lee Clinton, who was not at home. The dispatch explained the attack by saying the two men had talked disrespectfully of white women, and it ran in New York dailies and in Southern weekly news columns.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Figures and Cicero Green
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Figures and Cicero Green took place on the night of July 21, 1885, when about one hundred armed men on horseback rode into Minden, Louisiana, and shot the two Black prisoners to death inside the town jail. The two men were held on accusations of murder, and the mob also took a number of townspeople prisoner, among them a local newspaper editor. The killing was carried in Louisiana papers and in brief wire items as far away as Nevada and Rhode Island.

episodes.title: Lynching of Peter Stamps
episodes.lead: The lynching of Peter Stamps took place at Douglasville, Georgia, in late July 1885, when a mob reported at 500 men took Stamps, a Black man, from custody and hanged him at a railroad bridge. Stamps had been jailed after Ida Abercrombie, the daughter of a white farmer, named him as the father of her expected child, and the mob formed after she died in convulsions. Newspapers across the country carried the case as a one-line brief, while the fullest dispatch added that strychnine was found in the girl's body and that her death might have been suicide.

episodes.title: Killing of Warren Bennett
episodes.lead: The killing of Warren Bennett was the shooting of a Black youth of about sixteen while he hoed cotton at the Hickory Tavern Crossroads in Laurens County, South Carolina, on the morning of July 9, 1885. A coroner's jury returned a verdict against persons unknown, and a murder warrant later sworn out against a young white man, Wade Bolt, led to no reported arrest. The News and Courier made the case a centerpiece of its investigation of lawlessness in Laurens County, calling it one of the most atrocious crimes ever committed in the State.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Anderson at Danville, Kentucky
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Anderson at Danville, Kentucky, took place on a Saturday night, probably August 1, 1885, when a mob went to the Danville jail to hang Anderson, a Black man accused of assaulting Mrs. J. H. Hiatt. The jailer had hidden him, and he was later moved to Harrodsburg and Lexington. The Stanford Semi-Weekly Interior Journal used the failure to condemn mobs.

episodes.title: Canton, Texas, night shootings (1885)
episodes.lead: The Canton, Texas, night shootings were a series of attacks in early August 1885 in and near Canton, in Van Zandt County, in which armed white men fired into Black homes at night, wounding Ben Fullbright and killing Bob Prewitt. A coroner's jury attributed Prewitt's death to a resident of Canton, but no arrest was reported, and the Dallas Herald's correspondent described local officials as unable or unwilling to act.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Embry, Johnson and Hanesford
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Embry, Johnson and Hanesford took place on the night of Saturday, 1 August 1885, when a mob planned to take three Black prisoners from the jail at Stanford, Lincoln County, Kentucky, and hang them. After a delegation of Black men offered to guard the jail, Judge Varnon had the sheriff and jailer take the prisoners away, and no one was harmed. The Stanford Interior Journal, the only paper found to name the prisoners, used the episode to condemn mob violence against prisoners already held by the law.

episodes.title: Killing of a Black man in Humphreys County, Tennessee (1885)
episodes.lead: The killing of a Black man in Humphreys County, Tennessee, took place shortly before Nashville dispatches of August 22-23, 1885, reported it, when a crowd that meant to beat him shot him as he tried to escape. His body was found the next morning near his cabin, and no one was arrested. The killing reached the press only as background to a Nashville dispatch on the whipping of Black residents by disguised men, which white and Black papers ran under 'Ku-Klux' headlines.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of George Mack in Huntingdon, Pennsylvania
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of George Mack took place in Huntingdon, Pennsylvania, in August 1885, after Mack, a Black circus worker some papers called Mock, was jailed on a charge of joining in an assault on a girl near the grounds of Cole's circus on August 10. Dispatches reported "strong talk" and "wild talk" of lynching him, and a later wire said mob violence was "loudly threatened" against him and a second accused man in the same jail. No attack was reported, and by late August Mack was awaiting trial.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Samuel B. Goode
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Samuel B. Goode took place in New York City on August 22, 1885, when a crowd yelled "Lynch him" and "Kill the black hound" as Goode, a Black man accused of stabbing Policeman James North to death, was taken to the Tombs. Goode was not harmed and was committed without bail, and a coroner's jury later found that North died of a stab wound inflicted by him. The New York papers dwelt more on the police captain's view, echoed by the Dispatch and the Black New York Freeman, that North provoked the fight by slapping, kicking and clubbing Goode.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Davis
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Davis took place in the early morning of August 9, 1885, when a crowd of masked men broke into the jail at Cuthbert, Georgia, took out Davis, a 19-year-old Black man, and hanged and shot him at a nearby railroad bridge. Davis had been charged with assaulting Sylvia Knight, the nine-year-old daughter of a Baptist minister, two days earlier. The story ran in papers from Savannah to Dakota Territory, and white papers presented the killing as deserved punishment.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Cooper
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Cooper took place on the night of about August 18, 1885, when a mob went to the house of Cooper, a Black man, in the Seventeenth District of Madison County, Tennessee, and shot him dead. The mob also wounded Jack Allison, a young white man, who was expected to die, and no arrests had been made two days later.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jake Evans
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jake Evans was the hanging of a Black man by a mob at Auburn, Alabama, in the summer of 1885, after he was arrested on an accusation of assaulting a white woman. According to the only report found, the mob overpowered the officers who held him and hanged him to a tree. The event is known from a single wire paragraph that ran in two Dakota weeklies between August and September 1885.

episodes.title: Whipping of Kate Brown
episodes.lead: The whipping of Kate Brown was an assault on a Black woman at Hillsboro, Caroline County, Maryland, on August 3, 1885, when two white men dragged her from a magistrate's office and whipped her. She had been waiting there for their trial on a charge of beating her in her own house a few days earlier. The only known account, a Baltimore letter in the New York Freeman, presented the case as one of several outrages against Black Marylanders that the white press ignored.

episodes.title: Keyport store riot (1885)
episodes.lead: The Keyport store riot was a Saturday-night attack in August 1885 in which a gang of men from the Big Woods chased a man into a store kept by Black people in Keyport, New Jersey, assaulted the proprietor and broke in the store front. The fight became a melee of brickbats, a thrown bottle and three shots from the store's side, and warrants were issued against the attackers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Lawrence
episodes.lead: The lynching of Lawrence was the hanging of a Black man accused of rape by a "company of men" within the limits of Girard, Kansas, some time before mid-August 1885. It drew notice because a mass meeting of citizens of nearby Baxter Springs adopted resolutions formally approving the hanging and thanking those who carried it out.

episodes.title: Turning back of the Elberton colored band from Madison County, Georgia
episodes.lead: The turning back of the Elberton colored band from Madison County, Georgia, occurred in August 1885, when a Black band hired by Madison county prohibitionists to play on election day was told on arrival that it would be safer to go home, and left. No violence was reported, and the account survives only as a brief paragraph from the Elberton Gazette reprinted in the Savannah Morning News on 22 August.

episodes.title: Lynching of an unnamed Black man at Oxford, Mississippi (1885)
episodes.lead: The lynching of an unnamed Black man at Oxford, Mississippi, took place in or shortly before early August 1885, after he was accused of having "attempted an outrage." It is known only from a one-sentence item in a Tennessee weekly, which gave no name, date, perpetrators or method.

episodes.title: Beating of Pearl at the Avondale picnic
episodes.lead: The beating of Pearl at the Avondale picnic was a crowd attack on a Black man at a picnic of Baltimore and Ohio railroad employees at Avondale, on the Licking Reservoir in Ohio, on Saturday, August 29, 1885. According to the only report found, Pearl had struck a white man and was then "assaulted by the crowd and terribly beaten."

episodes.title: Whipping of Richard Hindsman
episodes.lead: The whipping of Richard Hindsman was an assault in Villa Rica, Georgia, reported on August 9, 1885, in which white residents described as "indignant white citizens" gave a Black man three hundred lashes on the claim that he had insulted a white woman. The coverage consisted of a single Atlanta dispatch reprinted across the country, and it reports no arrests or legal proceedings. The case drew an editorial from the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, which condemned the whipping as a usurpation of the law and an instance of unequal justice for Black people.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ross Hollis
episodes.lead: The lynching of Ross Hollis was the hanging of Ross Hollis, a Black corporal of the Twenty-fifth United States Infantry at Fort Meade, by a mob at Sturgis, Dakota Territory, in late August 1885. Hollis was accused of shooting Dr. H. P. Lynch, a Sturgis physician, and after a coroner's jury returned a verdict against him he was taken from the town calaboose and hanged. White papers carried the story as swift punishment for an "assassination," and a second dispatch reported that armed Black soldiers had threatened to burn the town.

episodes.title: Whipping of Samuel Low and West Regan
episodes.lead: The whipping of Samuel Low and West Regan was an attack by seven disguised men on two Black men in the Duck River bottom of Humphreys County, Tennessee, on Friday, August 21, 1885. Low was given more than one hundred blows with ironwood switches, and Regan was beaten and driven from the county. Wire dispatches from Nashville presented the attack as one of a series of "Ku-Klux outrages" in the county, and the story was reprinted from New York to Minnesota and in the Black weekly Cleveland Gazette.

episodes.title: Lynching of Tom Tarver
episodes.lead: The lynching of Tom Tarver (also reported as Tom Carver and Tom Turner) took place in Dalton, Georgia, on the night of August 19, 1885, when about fifty masked "Regulators" raided houses they called disreputable, whipped several Black and white residents, and killed Tarver, a Black man. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of unknown parties, and no arrests were reported. The raid ran nationally under "Ku Klux" headlines, with sharply different accounts of how Tarver died.

episodes.title: Masked-band attack on Wallace Thompson's home in Lee County, Alabama
episodes.lead: The masked-band attack on Wallace Thompson's home was a night raid in late August 1885 on a farm about four miles from Columbus, Georgia, in Lee County, Alabama. Masked men broke into Thompson's house, chased him into the dark and whipped several Black people on his place to make them tell where he had gone. Thompson sold his property and fled across the river to Georgia; the only known report rests on his own account.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Wyatt Jones
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Wyatt Jones took place in August 1885 near Lynchburg, Harris County, Texas, when residents hunted Jones, a Black man accused of raping a white girl, intending to lynch him. Jones was instead captured by two Black men and brought to the Houston jail, where the sheriff was expected to hold him to keep him out of the townspeople's hands.
